extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate practitioners, IP litigators, and law students studying Federal Circuit patent procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards applied by the Federal Circuit in patent litigation and related proceedings (Section 337 domestic industry, issue preclusion, collateral estoppel, claim construction, exceptional case fees, pleading standards, finality vs. PTO proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 337 domestic industry economic prong
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain relief under Section 337 a complainant must show that 'an industry in the United States, relating to the articles protected by the patent, ... exists or is in the process of being established.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investments must relate to articles protected by a particular patent; the inquiry looks to 'sufficiently substantial investment in the exploitation of the intellectual property.' The Commission may attribute R&D/engineering investments directly to functionality necessary to practice patent elements. Aggregating investments across products that practice different patents can fail to provide an adequate basis to evaluate significance with respect to each asserted patent; where products practice different patents, the complainant must establish separate domestic industries for each group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation/aggregation rule for domestic industry investments
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenditures may not be aggregated across domestic products that practice different patents without allocation to the patents or product groups each asserted patent covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission expects evidence enabling evaluation of investments 'with respect to the articles protected by the patent.' Aggregating investments across products practicing different patents fails when it prevents assessment of significance of investments for each asserted patent; where products or product groups practice different patents, separate domestic-industry showings are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of R&D/expenditure testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Witness statements attributing R&D or other expenditures must have documentary support and an explanation of how figures were derived; mere estimates without support are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJ credibility determinations and weighing of evidence are entitled to great weight; courts will affirm findings that expenditures evidence is unreliable when based on unsupported estimations or lack documentary corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue preclusion / merger of interlocutory orders (Hartley principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a district court issues a final judgment, interlocutory orders merge with that final judgment and can have preclusive effect in later litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party's failure to appeal or seek vacatur of an interlocutory judgment (e.g., summary judgment of invalidity) before a dismissal with prejudice can render that interlocutory ruling preclusive against the patentee in later suits against different defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver/abandonment of doctrine-of-equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee's strategic abandonment or waiver of a doctrine-of-equivalents theory in earlier litigation precludes later assertion of that theory, even if claim construction later changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative abandonment for strategic reasons unrelated to claim construction constitutes waiver; failure to present the theory to the jury where strategically abandoned cannot be undone by later litigation over materially similar products.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Essentially the same’ products test for preclusion/Kessler doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused devices are 'essentially the same' where differences between them are merely colorable or unrelated to the limitations in the claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If products are essentially the same, Kessler may grant a product noninfringing status that carries to subsequent versions absent material differences. Courts review district findings for clear error on whether products are essentially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kessler doctrine scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Kessler grants a product a noninfringing status that prevents repeated harassment for continuing its business as usual post-final judgment; that noninfringing status can apply to subsequent versions of the originally accused products if there are 'no material differences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kessler fills the gap between claim and issue preclusion doctrines by protecting adjudged non-infringers; courts examine prior precedent to determine Kessler's applicability based on product similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel (Eleventh Circuit four-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral estoppel requires: (1) the issue at stake must be identical to the one involved in the prior litigation; (2) the issue must have been actually litigated in the prior suit; (3) the determination of the issue in the prior litigation must have been a critical and necessary part of the judgment; and (4) the party against whom the earlier decision is asserted must have had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit applies regional law for collateral estoppel issues; for patent-unique questions (e.g., whether claims are the same), the Federal Circuit applies its own law.

rubrics_metrics.name: District courts must perform claim construction (intrinsic evidence focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding two suits present the same infringement issue for preclusion purposes, the district court must assess claim scope by conducting a proper claim construction using intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on extrinsic evidence (expert reports) in place of intrinsic claim construction is error. The appellate court is ill-positioned to conduct claim construction in the first instance when parties have not provided claim construction briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel and differing burdens (IPR vs district court)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding underlying an unpatentability decision in an IPR (preponderance standard) does not automatically collaterally estop a patentee from making validity arguments in district court where a different legal standard (clear and convincing) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral estoppel may not apply where the second action involves application of a different legal standard; courts have distinguished cases where a claim was found unpatentable and affirmed (which may bar assertion) from those where claims were not found unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to expert testimony exclusion on factual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacks on the correctness of the facts in expert testimony generally go to the weight of the testimony and are for the jury to resolve, not a basis for exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts erred when excluding testimony because purported factual attacks should be addressed to credibility and not resolved by excluding the expert where factual disputes remain for the factfinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality standard for immunity from subsequent PTO unpatentability (Fresenius II test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment is 'sufficiently final' and immune to subsequent PTO unpatentability findings only if the litigation is entirely concluded such that the cause of action was merged into a final judgment that ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a remand requires more than merely executing judgment (e.g., recalculating damages, determining enhancement effects), the judgment is not final and remains subject to intervening PTO determinations. Finality is a bright-line: anything left to do other than execute the judgment means not final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional case inquiry under 35 U.S.C. § 285
rubrics_metrics.description: A case may be 'exceptional' and warrant attorneys' fees where the substantive strength of the infringement position is weak and the patentee continued to litigate despite objective baselessness (e.g., prosecution history disclaimer, public information showing noninfringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider prosecution history, public information, and whether the patentee persisted after being put on notice of baselessness. District courts have discretion but their factual findings on exceptionality are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on recovery of fees under § 285 for PTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: § 285 does not entitle a prevailing party to recover attorneys' fees incurred in parallel IPR proceedings that the party voluntarily pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery of fees for PTO proceedings may be permitted when participation was not optional (e.g., reissue proceedings initiated by the patent owner), but where a party voluntarily elected PTAB proceedings, § 285 does not support awarding IPR fees. Distinguish prior cases (e.g., PPG) based on who initiated the PTO proceeding and whether participation was optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of counsel for fees under § 285
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for attorney fees under § 285 does not extend to counsel or law firms; § 285 is silent as to who is liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts point to other statutes or rules (28 U.S.C. § 1927, Fed. R. Civ. P. 11) that expressly permit sanctions against attorneys; absence of such language in § 285 supports that it does not impose liability on counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-presentation principle and limits on courts raising unpled issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the adversary system, courts rely on parties to frame issues for decision; a district court abuses its discretion by rendering a decision on a ground not raised by the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not decide issues (e.g., § 101 eligibility) that the parties did not brief or argue at trial or in post-trial briefing. Parties' presentation shapes the issues the court adjudicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity under § 282 applies to § 101 challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 282's presumption that a patent is valid and the requirement that invalidity be shown by clear and convincing evidence applies to all grounds of validity, including § 101 patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must apply the presumption of validity rather than treat § 101 as a special threshold the court must address sua sponte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading standard for patent infringement at the motion-to-dismiss stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent plaintiff is not required to plead infringement on an element-by-element basis; the complaint must place the accused infringer on notice of the accused activity and plausibly allege infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review of district court categorizations of allegations as well-pleaded factual (entitled to presumption of truth) versus conclusory is de novo. Detailed infringement theory and claim charts, along with the technology's simplicity, can satisfy notice pleading. Defendants' operational roles that are contested factual issues cannot be resolved at dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading indirect infringement and intent at motion-to-dismiss
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff pleading indirect (induced) infringement need not identify a specific induced customer; promotional materials, brochures, and allegations of support/instructions can plausibly infer induced direct infringement and the requisite intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations that defendant provided support, instructions, or promotional materials that enable infringement can suffice to plead intent; specificity as to a particular customer is not strictly required at the pleading stage.
